Annual Report 
For the Year Ending April SOth, 1922 


The Young Men’s Christian Association of Montreal. 


Characteristics of Period. 

The past year in the life of the Montreal Young Men’s Christian 
Association was one in which the stability of our work was severely 
tested by the changing world-wide economic conditions with a consequent 
period of deflation and depression. Unusually heavy demands were 
made upon our organization due to unemployment and the large amount 
of leisure time which men out of work had on their hands. 

The difficulty of securing adequate financial support for our work 
was many times greater than for some years. 

We are profoundly grateful to our Heavenly Father for His guid- 
ance in our endeavor to conserve the important advances gained during 
the past ten years. 


Re-Examination of Policies 

Your directors have found it necessary to re-examine our policies 
and tendencies, some of which were developed during times of pros- 
perity, and it is with a new conviction that we now re-state eight of the 
essential principles upon which our entire work is based. 


(1) CENTRAL OBJECTIVE-- The purpose of the Young Men’s 
Christian Association is the winning of men and boys to Jesus Christ and 
to enlist and train them in Christian service. No activity in our pro- 
gramme which does not have this as its ultimate aim can be worthily 
undertaken. 


(2) FOURFOLD WORK -- Every Branch of the Association 
should do a fourfold work -- Educational, Physical, Social and Religious 
-- to build symmetrical Christian character in men and boys, and give 
opportunity for its expression. Many leaders to-day think that the Re- 
ligious activities should not be a department of our work but a feature 
of EACH department. On any basis, it is important to carry through a 
Religious Work programme with both individuals and groups. 


(3) VOLUNTEER CONTROL AND LEADERSHIP -- The 
Association activities should be determined, managed, and carried through 
by volunteer laymen through a system of Officers, Directors, and Com- 
mitteemen assisting the Employed Officers in the leadership of the organ- 
ization and its work. It has been more obvious than ever before that 
this principle must be applied through our entire organization. The most 
efficient group of Employed Officers cannot make permanent this work 
without a full measure of leadership and control by volunteers. 


(4) SKILLED PROFESSIONAL LEADERSHIP -- Expert em- 
ployed executive officers are indispensable to the proper promotion and 


3 


development of the modern Young Men’s Christian Association. These 
Employed Officers should be technically trained in Association history, 
principles and methods, in addition to-having a well rounded general 
education and, if possible, some business experience. The Association 
Secretary should know the history and BiESneny: of the Movement and 
‘his own function. 

(5) METROPOLITAN PLAN OF ORGANIZATION -- There 
should be only one Young Men’s Christian Association in each city. 
The various fields within the city are occupied by Branches all operated 
under the authority and direction of a common Board of Directors. The 
detailed administration of each Branch is in the hands of a Board of 
Management approved by the Metropolitan Board of Directors. Among 
the beneficial results of this form of organization are:- 

(a) Comprehensive and Unified City-Wide Policies. 

(b) Economy in Business Administration. 

(c) More Adequate Supervision. 

(d) Greater Confidence and Support of Citizens. 

(e) Stability. 

(f) The preservation of Local Autonomy in Branches. 

(6) BUILDING AND NON-BUILDING WORK-- As a Christian 
Civic Enterprise, the Association cannot confine its activities to its Build- 
ings. It has a wonderful opportunity to co-operate with the school, the 
Church, the Home, the State, and Industry in all points of a community. 
Christ’s principle, that an individual who saves his life shall lose it, is 
applicable to Movements. When the Y.M.C.A. seeks to loose itself in a 
community it will find itself. 


(7) FINANCIAL SUPPORT -- The Association is not expected 
to be self-supporting. The Directors of any successful Association must 
secure subscriptions annually to meet the cost of : 

(a) Boys Work. 

(b) Work in Non-Building Branches. 

(c) Many activities for which there is no 

charge to the public or members. 

(d) Adequate upkeep of Buildings, repairs, 

and alterations. 

(8) WORLD WIDE EXTENSION -- We are under moral and 
spiritual obligation to extend our work into unoccupied centres in Canada 
and non-Christian lands. We have a stewardship of methods, money, 
men and ideals. We owe it to our members to interest them in the big 
enterprise of Home and Foreign Missions. 


Financial Summary. 


The policy of an aggressive promotion of all our services through- 
out the year, combined with rigid economy in administration, has result- 
ed in the reduction of $33,608.03 in the amount required from interested 
friends by way of subscriptions. 

The Treasurer’s report will show a gross expenditure during the 
year of $317,106.24, of which $67,298.97 was received in subscriptions 
as compared with $100,907.00 last year. 


4 


It, should be carefully noted that this saving in subscriptions has 
been. largely effected by merging the work in Maisonneuve with that of 
the Eastern District; and the Community Work in Point St. Charles 
with that of the Railroad Branch; by increased earnings from dormitory 
and membership fees; by effecting economies in building administration. 
The re-organization of the National Council on a peace time basis has 
reduced our share of the National Budget by a considerable amount. 


We have not abandoned any piece of Association work in any sec- 
tion of this great city, and it is a source of satisfaction that it has been 
possible to even extend our service throughout Cote St. Paul and Ville 
Emard as well as in the St. James-St. Antoine district. 

It has been possibile, also, to maintain full staffs and programmes 
in all established Branches. 

Notwithstanding the large reduction in our subscription budget, 
the task of securing same was an arduous one. A Special Names Canvass 
was held in June, and a regularly organized campaign was set up in Octo- 
ber. In addition to these efforts, the Finance Committe of the Branches 
worked steadily from November to May under the leadership of Mr. 
Rufus C. Holden, Chairman of the Metropolitan Finance Committee. 
The latter has been indefatigable in his personal effort to build up 
a living endowment for the Association in the form of a ‘Civic 
Membership” list, which, on April 30th, totalled 278. The reception 
accorded the presentation of our work to individuals and corporations 
was most gratifying and speaks volumes for the place of the Association 
in our city. 


Retirement Plan. 


A practical and scientifically devised plan for increasing the effi- 
ciency and stabilizing the service of the Y.M.C.A. Employed Officers 
is to be set in motion on July 1st, the four million dollars having been 
practically all raised. 

It will be recalled that Mr. John D. Rockefeller, Jr., just before he 
started upon his recent trip to China, made a contribution of one million 
dollars to inaugurate the Fund. 

Dr. Mott made a sporting proposition to his associates in the Secre- 
taryship last June. If they would subscribe a quarter of a million from 
their own pockets he woujd raise it to a million from a few 
large gifts privately secured. The Secretaries responded with gifts 
exceeding $300,000.00 and Dr. Mott in nine subscriptions secured 
the balance. 

The second two millions was assigned to local Associations across 
the Continent and victory is now assured. 

Under the leadership of Dr. John W. Ross and Lt. Col. Gerald W. 
Birks, Montreal exceeded her objective of $50,000.00 and raised $57,805.- 
00. Of this amount $25,000.00 was given by one generous friend. 

The International Committee has definitely decided to retire all 
Employed Officers sixty years of age or over as soon as this plan becomes 
effective. 

All the victories in our financial undertakings thus far have come 
in the pathway of unselfishness. We refer not only to the generous 


5 


subscriptions received but more especially to the unselfishness of Assecia- 
tion workers who have been willing to put aside personal interests and 
plans in order that this Kingdom task may be accomplished. 


Centralized Accounting. 

The centralization of our accounting and financing, which was 
inaugurated on May 1st, has been an unqualified success, and has result- 
ed in unifying the administration of our entire work besides effecting 
economies in many directions. The Association owes a debt of gratitude 
to Mr. A.D. Anderson for his untiring efforts in this department. 


Membership 

It is no longer possible to measure the Association’s service by 
the number of men and boys in our membership and yet this must always 
bear a direct relation to the strength of any organization. Our member- 
ship on April 30th was as follows:-

Approximately seven thousand different men and boys have been 
members during the year but due to unemployment, removal from the 
city and other reasons, many have not renewed their membership. 

Prior to the war the membership of the North America Y.M.C.A.’s 
totalled approximately 600,000. It is now in excess of 900,000. A de- 
termined effort is being made to increase this to one million by next 
November. Will Montreal accept her share of responsibility in this 
Million Member Movement ? 

Much study has been made recently on the subject of membership, 
and the table above indicates the age groups within our Association. 
The following is laid down by the Association of Membership Secretaries 


as a kasis for a balanced membership:-

Central, Westmount, North and Railroad Branches. 


It is not proposed to deal in this report with the manifold activi- 
ties of the Westmount, Railroad, North or Central Branches, all of 
which have already been covered in the reports of their several Annual 
Meetings and which have received much publicity in the daily press. 


CENTRAL BRANCH -- The place of our Central Branchin the 
life of this great city is a large one and. its record of service in meeting 
the needs of both resident and transient young men measures up to the 
expectations of those who were responsible for its erection. 

Progress has been made towards its being self-sustaining and the 
budget for next year contemplates a grant from the Joint Fund of only 
$2,500.00 or 1 1-2% of the gross expenditure. 

Attention is called to the great opportunity for service among the 
Business and Professional men in the city which could be reached more 
adequately by the provision of better dressing room accommodation 
in the Physical Department. This would involve an expenditure of a 
considerable amount but is worthy of a serious consideration by the 
Central Board of Management and the Metropolitan Board. 


WESTMOUNT BRANCH -- The Westmount Branch has made 
two important changes in policy during the year: 

1) The organization of a Junior Board of Management, the development 
of this idea is now occupying the attention of the forward looking 
men in our Movement. 

(2) The opening of a Branch of the Association’s work in the St James- 
St. Antoine district, where, beginning with twenty-five boys, over 
135 are now being reached in Association activities. 


NORTH BRANCH-- Under the leadership of Mr. W.J.Holliday, 
who rejoined the Association forces last June, the work in the North End 
Branch has been steadily regaining the strong position it held in the early 
days of the war. 


RAILROAD BRANCH -- In addition to carrying on a most use- 
ful programme of work for boys and men in the Railroad Branch at Point 
St. Charles, the Board has taken responsibility for the work pioneered 
in the community during 1920-1921. Although the building is quite 
inadequate to meet the situation there, the work is being carried forward 
courageously until such time as conditions make possible a building 
extension programme. 

All three Buildings have been well maintained during the year, 
expenditure on repairs, replacements and furnishings having been made 
in each one, and to-day they are in good condition. 


Non-Building or Community Branches. 


Y.M.C.A. services in sections of our city not reached by our Build- 
ings has long since passed the experimental stage, and its place in the 
community life has perhaps been even more largely realized this year, 
when there was so much unemployment and distress, than ever before. 


7 


COTEST. PAUL AND VILLE EMARD--Under the leadership of 
Mr. J.G. MacKinnon, our work was not only carried on within industrial 
plants but was projected throughout Ville Emard and Cote St. Paul. 
In this district, activities were carried on in the Hadley Street office; 
the Town Hall for concerts and movies; the Unos Hall for banquets 
movies, and inspirational meetings; the old Methodist Church for a gym- 
nasium; an open air skating rink; public and private playgrounds, 
and industrial plants. 


_ Space does not permit of our recording the industrial picnics, 
Christmas trees, athletic and social events which were carried through in 
co-operation with industries, Churches and Schools. 


Church accommodation in this district is totally inadequate and 
one of the largest contributions made to the life of the young men and 
boys has been co-operation with the Churches. 


In co-operation with the Canadian Car & Foundry Company, 
644 loads of wocd were distributed to families who were, in many cases, 
without fuel. Twelve hundred pounds of fish were distributed to over 
200 needy families on National Fish Day, and in co-operation with indus- 
tries, doctors’ bills and rent have been paid; and provisions, coal, wood, 
etc., supplied. 


It is generally recognized that it is not the function of the Asso- 
ciation to engage in any large amount of relief work, there being special 
agencies in the community organized for this purpose. It would appear, 
however, in the light of our recent experience that provided another 
winter reveals as much destitution, the Association should take a still more 
active share in this type of service in co-operation with other agencies. 
The work of the Family Welfare Association, St. Vincent de Paul, Kiwa- 
nis Club, Star Relief, Ex-Fighting Men’s Association, and St. George’s 
Society has meant everything in the lives of families where the bread 
winners were out of work. 


EASTERN DISTRICT -- In line with the policy of your Direct- 
ors to merge the work in Maisonneuve with District no. 4, the office 
on St. Urbain Street was closed and an attempt made to administer the 
work from Bleury Street east from our office on Adam Street. As the 
year progressed, it became apparent that this was not satisfactory, with 
the result that Mr. P. Jennens was engaged on part time to specialize 
in Boys’ Work in Maisonneuve, and new offices were rented by the Asso- 
ciation at the corner of Sanguinet and St. Catherine Streets. 


This move, which required a good deal of energy to carry through, 
is already proving to be invaluable and is co-ordinating many activities 
in the foreign speaking districts. 


Throughout the year educational and gymnasium classes and 
athletic events have been conducted in Alexandra School, and an excel- 
lent piece of Boy Scout work has been done with the Italian and Syrian 
boys. Mr. Burgoyne reports real growth in citizenship and character 
among many employed boys of foreign parentage with whom he has now 
been working for two years. Much constructive work has been done in 
co-operation with the Juvenile Court and other agencies, including re- 
lief work. 

8 


During the year many agencies have been used for our Boys’ 
Work, including Churches, the Macdonald Playground, Fletcher’s 
Field, tennis courts, Maisonneuve Protestant School, and Camp Lewis. 

VERDUN -- The Association’s work in Verdun is now in its 
third year and covers an extensive field of activity with the boys of the 
city. The night school has completed a favorable year and it is propos- 
ed to continue this type of service among the boys of the community 
who are employed during the day. 

The Association Secretary has complete charge of the gymnasium 
training of all boys in the Protestant Schools from the 6th grade up, and 
takes entire charge of the field athletics for the four Schools. The four 
Protestant Churches have combined in a recreational programme for 
their boys and the Secretary has had charge of these groups two evenings 
per week. 

Camps 

KANAWANA -- Kamp Kanawana was open last season from 
June 22nd to August 27th. The registration this year constituted a new 
record, with a total of 391 boys as compared with 289 in 1921. The 
largest number in camp at any one time was 212. Registration 
by Branches:- Unattached 16; Verdun 12; North Branch 73; West- 
mount 130; Central 160. 

The activities of the camp are in line with the purpose of the Young 
Men’s Christian Association. They are fourfold in character. A total 
of 812 badges were won by the boys for proficiency in the following 
subjects:- Camp improvement 65; life saving 30; rowing 38; beginners’ 
swimming 20; hikes 105; resuscitation 35; wood craft 20; bandaging 20; 
simple remedies 26; basketry 30. 

The Royal Life Saving Society held an examination of the boys 
in Camp at which seven won the award of merit; 23 won the proficiency 
medal; 15, the bronze medallion; and 2 received the honor instruction 
badges. 

CAMP OTOREKE-- The Camp for men was again conducted dur- 
ing the months of July and August, the attendance being somewhat less 
than the year previous. Numbers from the various Branches are as 
follows:- Visitors 9; Westmount 11; North Branch 17; Central 82; total 
126, as compared with 216 in 1920. 

A new tennis court was added to the Camp equipment this year. 

After careful consideration, it was the decision of your Directors 
that this Camp be not opened during the present year. It is generally 
recognized that it has not the same interest for our younger members 
that it had some years ago. 

CADET CAMP, POINTE AUX TREMBLES--During the month 
of July, the Association conducted a programme for the boys in the Mili- 
tia Cadet Camp at Pointe aux Trembles. Mr. J.G. MacKinnon was in 
charge, and this service was greatly appreciated and generously acknow- 
ledged by the General Officer commanding District No. 4. 

Foreign Work. 

The first Foreign Secretaries of the Movement were sent in 1889-- 
David McConaughy to India, and John T. Swift to Japan. Since then 
the number has increased to approximately 200. Now, as the result of 
their training of leaders, there are associated with them more than 500

Chartered Accountants. 


Montreal, May 22nd, 1922. 


native Secretaries. The policy of the Association is to establish model 
Associations in influential cities. Already about eighty of the commer- 
cial, educational and political capitals of the world outside North America 
have been entered. Is it not true ‘‘As go the Cities, so go the Nations ?” 

The money from Canada and the United States is spent only for 
the support of our own Secretaries and their families. All current ex- 
penses of foreign local Associations are raised in their respective cities. 
For example, in 1920 North America invested in Y.M.C.A. work in China 
$520,512.00, and China matched this with $704,247.00. 

Last year Canada’s contributions to the Foreign Work were 
$40,338.00 as compared with $55,219.00 in 1920. Of this amount Mont- 
real subscribed $14,795.53 as compared with $21,172.33 in 1920. 

Collections were made by our Branches as follows: 

Central $1,625.82; Westmount $374.35; North End $333.65; Railroad 
$105.50. 

Montreal should have a larger place in this work. Every member 
should be a subscriber. The Foreign Work is the finest antidote for 
Provincialism-- It broadens the thinking of members; prepares them to 
be better world citizens, and brings spiritual reactions which tone up 
the life of the whole Association. 

The following Canadians are serving the Association abroad:- 

BRAZIL: 

D. G. Magee --Rio de Janeiro. 
CANAL ZONE: 

F. N. Whittaker --Balboa. 
CEYLON: 

W. Murray Brooks-- Colombo. 

W. Gordon Brown -- Colombo. 


CHINA: 
L. E. McLachlin -- Foochow. 
J. L.McPherson -- Hongkong. 
H. R.Sweetman -- Nanking. 
J. H. Geldart------ Shangai. 
A. Lockley -------- Tientsin. 
G. H. Cole --------- Shangai. 
INDIA: 
M. W. Harlow ---- Allahabad. 
C. S. Paterson----- Calcutta. 
H. G. Beall -------- Hyderabad. 
J. D. Omond------ Jubbulpore. 
L. S. Dixon -------- Travancore. 
A. P. Park --------- Patna. 
JAPAN: 
G. E. Trueman --- Nagoya.. 
G. S. Patterson --- Tokio.

Dr. J. H. Gray --National Physical Director, China. 


14 


Visit of Lord Byng 


We were signally honored in the month of January by having a 
visit from the Governor General, Lord Byng of Vimy, on the occasion of 
the Annual Dinner of the National Council. His Excellency accepted 
an Honorary Membership in the Montreal Association and responded 
to the presentation by the President, Mr. A. O. Dawson, ina most inspir- 
ing manner. He made a tour of inspection of the work in the Central 
Building and congratulated the Association upon the effectiveness of 
its service. 


Obituary 
We mourn the loss of the following men who gave of themselves 
unsparingly in the Association service. The following resolutions passed 


by the Board of Directors indicate the esteem and love in which they were 
held. 


Mr. D. W. ROSS sIR JOHN KENNEDY 


MR. W. H. HENDERSON Mr. SAMUEL PUGH 


EERE AED WS TDRSS SEE NIE PSE LE REIS ESS DIRE DRESS E EE 


15 


Resolved: 


That this Board of Directors place on record the deep sense of 
loss we have sustained in the passing of our friend and co-worker, D.W. 
Ross, after a long and trying illness borne with Christian grace and pa- 
tience. 

As one of the oldest members of our Board, his interest in every- 
thing pertaining to the work of the Master, from the smallest matters of 
detail to the Presidency of the Association, never flagged for a moment. 

As a beloved companion whose genial cheery manner was ever 
and inspiration to those who had the privilege of meeting him, and as 
a generous warmhearted friend and wise counsellor whose judgment and 
advice were ever tempered and inspired by his love for his Master and his 
fellow men, we feel that the Association has met with an irreparable loss. 

We place upon our records our appreciation of his great worth 
and express to his bereaved family our sorrow and sympathy in their 
affliction. 

Resolved: 

That this Board records its profound sorrow in the passing away 
of Sir John Kennedy, the eminent Engineer who for forty-six years was 
connected with the Harbor of Montreal and who, though blind, rendered 
most faithful and loyal service as a Director of this Association for nearly 
forty years. His deep interest in the Association, and faithful attendance 
at all meetings of the Board were a source of great inspiration to his 
fellow Directors and the employed officers. We extend to Lady Kennedy 
and family sympathy in their irreparable loss. 


Resolved: 

That this Board expresses its profound sorrow in the loss of Mr.S. 
Pugh, who was a member of the Railroad Y.M.C.A. from its inception, 
and who for fifteen years rendered most faithful service as a member 
of the Board of Management in Point St. Charles. His radiant Christian 
life and his spirit of sacrificial service meant much to the extension of 
Christ’s Kingdom among young men and boys. We extend to Mrs. 
Pugh and family our deepest sympathy in their great loss. 


Resolved: 

That this Board records its high appreciation of the great worth 
of Mr. Wm. H. Henderson, who served the Association in this city with 
such marked unselfishness and high purpose. As Educational Director, 
and later as Executive Secretary of the Central Branch, his devotion to 
the cause of our Master was such as to make him beloved by all, and es- 
pecially by hundreds of young men whom he befriended in their time of 
great need. We extend to Mrs. Henderson and daughter our deepest 
sympathy in their irreparable loss. 


We are sorry to record, also the following deaths among our 
subscribers during the year:- 


Andrew Baile. Geo. Boulter. Dr. J.M. Elder. 
Dr. Ed. J. O’Connor. H. W. Phillips T. H. Rieder. 

Jas. Robinson. Dr.Herbert Symonds. Henry Munderloh. 
Sir Frederick Orr-Lewis. Mrs. E. F. Ames. W. T. Rogers. 
Mrs. Jas. Alves. R. McD. Paterson. 


16 


Recruiting and Training for Christian Callings 


The Training Policy of the National Council, which enables men 
to train in McGill and Toronto, is one of the forward steps of the year 
and should have the heartiest backing of all Association men in Montreal. 


During the year, Employed Officers have been elert to discover 
young men for Christian callings, and Col. Birks was host recently at a 
Dinner to twelve young men who are being challenged to Life Service. 
Dr. John R. Mott says, ‘One thousand young men of conviction, 
religious zeal, personality, undiscourageable will power, strong physique 
and finest intellectual training are needed for the Association Secretary- 
ship.” This phase of Association work constitutes one of our greatest 
opportunities and obligations. 


Unsolved Problems. 


As we face the future there are some matters which appear to 
challenge our best thought and constructive endeavor. 


SUITABLE WAR MEMORIALS --Over three and a half years 
have now passed since the historic day when the armistice was signed 
which stopped for Canada the great loss of her young manhood whose 
lives were so heroically poured out during the Great War. The contribu- 
tion of the Montreal Young Men’s Christian Association was a notable 
one and some suitable war memorial should be placed in each of our 
Buildings at an early date. 


THE NEED FOR A VITAL MEMBERSHIP --It is doubtful if 
there has ever been a year in the history of our Movement when there 
was such a strong and apparent desire to improve our organization. 
One of the subjects causing our Leaders the most concern is that of vita- 
lizing our membership. Our Buildings are thronging with young people. 
In all parts of the city we are touching thousands of young men and boys. 
Let us face frankly certain questions. 


Are they privilege users or real members ? 

Are we firing them with common ideals and passion ? 

To what extent are we begetting in them the spirit of giving 
rather than getting? 

To what extent are we making them a united, aggressive force 
in Montreal and the world? 

Are we generating the spirit of the Crusaders ? 


THE PROBLEM OF YOUNGER MEN-- Notable advances have 
been made in the past few years in that section of our membership 
between 18 and 21 years of age. There is a growing conviction that 
new emphasis must be placed upon young men up to 25. Many experi- 
ments are being made notably in London, Ont., and Westmount, where 
Junior Boards of Management have been organized with excellent results. 


17 


There should be more strong and prophetic messages given to 
these young men who alone have the power of working out the solution 
of our problems during the next decade. 


BUILDING EXTENSION --The appeal from ministers, business 
men and others from many districts of our city for Y.M.C.A. Buildings 
is most difficult to resist. We are all familiar with the great need and 
opportunity in Point St. Charles, Verdun, Cote St. Paul and Ville Emard. 
The recent deputations from the East End, one of clergymen and the 
other of business men of great earnestness, indicate that right at our doors 
is a neglected field for a most Christlike ministry. Let us, therefore, 
hold in prominence these areas of neglect. 


The decision of the Rochester Association to erect new buildings 
of a modern type which can be operated by two employed officers is of 
deep interest to us. It would appear that their plan might well be 
studied by your Board. 


In closing this report may I refer to the spirit of harmony and good 
will which has characterized the Employed Officers, Board, and Commit- 
teemen in their united efforts for the expanding Kingdom.. 


With reverent gratitude, we recognise the place intercessory prayer 
has taken in all our work. What do we not owe to those friends who have 
shared the Prayer side of our common task ? 3 


Respectfully submitted, 


General Secretary
